article.title: Birthday Wishes in Punjabi: Choose the Script Before the Words
article.excerpt: Punjabi is written in Gurmukhi in India and Shahmukhi in Pakistan, so a birthday wish in Punjabi is really two messages. Eight wishes in Gurmukhi with transliteration and meaning, the honorifics elders expect, and a measured comparison against our 96-character median personal message.

faqs.question: How do you say happy birthday in Punjabi?
faqs.answer: The standard line is ਜਨਮਦਿਨ ਦੀਆਂ ਲੱਖ ਲੱਖ ਵਧਾਈਆਂ (janamdin diyan lakh lakh vadhaiyan), literally "a hundred thousand congratulations on your birthday". ਸਾਲਗਿਰਾ ਮੁਬਾਰਕ (salgira mubarak) is the shorter alternative and the one that also works in Pakistani Punjab.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Gurmukhi and Shahmukhi?
faqs.answer: They are two scripts for the same spoken language. Gurmukhi is used in Indian Punjab and has 41 letters; Shahmukhi is Perso-Arabic, used in Pakistani Punjab, and has 38. A reader of one usually cannot read the other.

faqs.question: Can a Punjabi speaker in Pakistan read a Gurmukhi birthday message?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Kulwindr Kaur's study of Punjabi cultural translation notes that the two populations cannot read or write each other's script even though they understand each other in speech. Send Shahmukhi or Roman instead.

faqs.question: Is it acceptable to write a Punjabi birthday wish in English letters?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is often the safest choice. A 2025 study of Punjabi–English social media text found many Punjabi users type in Roman on WhatsApp because the Gurmukhi character set is large and slow to type. Roman runs about 16% longer in characters, though.

faqs.question: Are Punjabi birthday wishes only for Sikhs?
faqs.answer: No. Punjabi is spoken by Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims across India and Pakistan, and it is the mother tongue of 44.15% of Pakistan's population. Gurmukhi has a Sikh origin, but the language is not religiously bounded.

faqs.question: What is the most respectful Punjabi birthday wish for an elder?
faqs.answer: ਤੁਹਾਨੂੰ ਜਨਮਦਿਨ ਦੀਆਂ ਬਹੁਤ ਬਹੁਤ ਵਧਾਈਆਂ ਜੀ (tuhanu janamdin diyan bahut bahut vadhaiyan ji). The plural tuhanu and the closing ji are what mark the respect; dropping either makes it read as casual.

faqs.question: Should I use tu or tusi in a birthday message?
faqs.answer: Use tusi for anyone older than you or senior to you, and tu only for a close friend, sibling or someone younger. Punjabi marks respect grammatically through the plural, so the wrong pronoun changes the meaning, not just the tone.

faqs.question: Why does my Punjabi wish show up as boxes or question marks?
faqs.answer: The device has no Gurmukhi font installed. It is more common on desktop than on phones, and 48.6% of birthday page views on SubhSandesh are mobile against 51.0% site-wide, so laptops matter here. Roman transliteration always renders.

faqs.question: How long should a Punjabi birthday wish be?
faqs.answer: Short. Across 198 birthday pages on SubhSandesh the median personal message is 96 characters, and 106 of 197 are under 100. Our eight Gurmukhi wishes average 31 characters, so three of them fit in that budget.

faqs.question: Is Salgira Mubarak Punjabi or Urdu?
faqs.answer: Both words are Persian-derived and are used in Punjabi as well as Urdu. That shared vocabulary is exactly why the phrase travels well between Indian and Pakistani Punjabi, where the more Sanskritic janamdin does not always.

faqs.question: What Punjabi birthday wish works for a brother or sister?
faqs.answer: ਮੇਰੇ ਵੀਰ ਨੂੰ ਜਨਮਦਿਨ ਦੀਆਂ ਲੱਖ ਵਧਾਈਆਂ (mere veer nu janamdin diyan lakh vadhaiyan) for a brother. Use bhaji for an elder brother and pehn for a sister — Punjabi has separate words for nearly every relation, and the exact one carries the affection.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Birthday Wishes in Punjabi: Choose the Script Before the Words

A birthday wish in Punjabi is two different objects, not one: Gurmukhi if the person reads Punjabi in India, Shahmukhi if they read it in Pakistan, and Roman Punjabi if they read neither. Get that wrong and the message is not badly worded, it is invisible. Keep it short, too: across 198 birthday pages built on SubhSandesh since April 2026, the median personal message is **96 characters** — about 15 words — and 106 of 197 messages come in under 100 characters.

The eight Punjabi wishes below average 31 characters in Gurmukhi, so three of them fit inside that median. Below: the wishes with sound and meaning, the script rule, the honorifics that decide whether an elder feels respected, and the framing almost every wishes page gets wrong.

## What a birthday wish in Punjabi actually is

Punjabi is one spoken language with two writing systems. Gurmukhi is used for the eastern dialects in Indian Punjab; Shahmukhi, built on the Perso-Arabic script, is used for the western dialects in Pakistani Punjab, as the peer-reviewed [Punjabi language snapshot in *Language Documentation and Description*](https://www.lddjournal.org/article/id/1239/) (2020) sets out.

They are not variants of one alphabet. Saini and Lehal count 41 letters in Gurmukhi — 38 consonants and three vowel bearers — against 38 in Shahmukhi, with different vowel machinery in each.

The practical consequence is blunt. Kulwindr Kaur's study of translating Punjabi cultural terms notes that the two populations "cannot read or write each other's language" even though they understand each other perfectly in speech.

So the spoken wish crosses the border. The written one does not: a Gurmukhi message pasted to a cousin in Lahore is a row of shapes.

## Eight birthday wishes in Punjabi, with script, sound and meaning

Each entry gives the Gurmukhi line, a Roman transliteration to read aloud, the English sense and who it suits. Character counts are on the Gurmukhi string.

### 1. The all-purpose one

**ਜਨਮਦਿਨ ਦੀਆਂ ਲੱਖ ਲੱਖ ਵਧਾਈਆਂ!** — *Janamdin diyan lakh lakh vadhaiyan!* — "A hundred thousand congratulations on your birthday." Twenty-seven characters, five words. The default for anyone: colleague, cousin, neighbour. No religious marker, no register risk, which makes it the safest line here when you are unsure of the relationship.

### 2. The one that works in Pakistan too

**ਸਾਲਗਿਰਾ ਮੁਬਾਰਕ ਹੋਵੇ!** — *Salgira mubarak hove!* — "Happy birthday." Twenty characters, three words. *Salgira* and *mubarak* are Persian-derived and current on both sides of the border, so it survives conversion to Shahmukhi intact. Use it for Pakistani Punjab, or any Punjabi-speaking Muslim family.

### 3. The one you say out loud

**ਜਨਮਦਿਨ ਮੁਬਾਰਕ, ਜੀਓ ਹਜ਼ਾਰਾਂ ਸਾਲ।** — *Janamdin mubarak, jio hazaaran saal.* — "Happy birthday, live a thousand years." Thirty-one characters. The second clause is a spoken blessing, not a card formula, so it reads warmer. Good for a voice note — it is what an aunt actually says at the door.

### 4. The respectful one for an elder

**ਤੁਹਾਨੂੰ ਜਨਮਦਿਨ ਦੀਆਂ ਬਹੁਤ ਬਹੁਤ ਵਧਾਈਆਂ ਜੀ।** — *Tuhanu janamdin diyan bahut bahut vadhaiyan ji.* — "Very many birthday congratulations to you." Forty characters, the longest here. Note *tuhanu*, not *tainu*, and the closing *ji*. For a parent, a teacher, a mother-in-law, or anyone notably older.

### 5. The religiously neutral blessing

**ਰੱਬ ਤੁਹਾਨੂੰ ਲੰਬੀ ਉਮਰ ਬਖ਼ਸ਼ੇ।** — *Rabb tuhanu lambi umar bakhshe.* — "May God grant you a long life." Twenty-eight characters. *Rabb* is used by Punjabi Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims alike, so reach for it when you do not know the family's faith — or when the group chat holds all three.

### 6. The Sikh blessing

**ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ ਤੁਹਾਡੀ ਉਮਰ ਲੰਬੀ ਕਰੇ।** — *Waheguru tuhadi umar lambi kare.* — "May Waheguru lengthen your life." Twenty-nine characters. *Waheguru* is specifically Sikh, and Kaur records the fuller Sikh salutation as a formula the more observant use. Send it to a Sikh household, never as a generic Punjabi wish.

### 7. The one for a brother or sister

**ਮੇਰੇ ਵੀਰ ਨੂੰ ਜਨਮਦਿਨ ਦੀਆਂ ਲੱਖ ਵਧਾਈਆਂ।** — *Mere veer nu janamdin diyan lakh vadhaiyan.* — "A hundred thousand birthday wishes to my brother." Thirty-six characters. Swap *veer* for *bhaji* if he is older, or *pehn* for a sister. The kinship word does the emotional work, so pick the exact one.

### 8. The one that sounds like a person

**ਜਿਉਂਦੇ ਰਹੋ, ਹੱਸਦੇ ਰਹੋ, ਜਨਮਦਿਨ ਮੁਬਾਰਕ!** — *Jiunde raho, hassde raho, janamdin mubarak!* — "Keep living, keep laughing, happy birthday." Thirty-seven characters. The plural imperative *raho* keeps it polite while the rhythm keeps it informal — a balance a copied line rarely strikes.

To give the wish somewhere to live, a [birthday page for parents](https://subhsandesh.in/birthday-parents) holds the Gurmukhi line, a photo and a voice note on one link — useful because the script problem disappears once the reader can hear you.

## Gurmukhi, Shahmukhi or Roman: pick before you write

Ask one question: where did the recipient learn to read? India means Gurmukhi, Pakistan means Shahmukhi, and diaspora — or don't know — means Roman.

Roman is not a cop-out. Singh and Kamboj's 2025 study of Punjabi–English social media text states plainly that because the Gurmukhi character set is large and typing it is slow, many Punjabi users write on WhatsApp, Facebook and Twitter in Roman script instead; their WhatsApp corpus runs to 311,271 sequences of 2 to 33 words.

There is a literacy layer under this. In a survey of 80 Punjabi speakers in Sargodha district, Pakistan, [Nazir, Aftab and Saeed](https://journals.uni-lj.si/ala/article/view/183) found younger speakers rated their Punjabi reading and writing at 25% while listening and speaking stayed strong. A native speaker who cannot read Punjabi is common.

And automated conversion is not a fix. Saini and Lehal at Punjabi University, Patiala, reported in 2011 that [20% of the 100 most frequent Shahmukhi words](https://learnpunjabi.org/pdf/WSD%20in%20Gurmukhi-Shahmukhi%20Trans.pdf) have more than one valid Gurmukhi reading, because Shahmukhi text carries short-vowel marks only 1.66% of the time against 6.13% in Gurmukhi. Their disambiguation algorithms reach just over 92% accuracy — good for research, not good enough for a name.

## How the three scripts compare on a 96-character message

We measured the eight wishes in all three renderings. Counts are code points; bytes are UTF-8.

| Rendering | Mean length | Mean UTF-8 bytes | Wishes inside 96 chars | Who reads it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gurmukhi | 31.0 chars | 82.8 | 3.1 | Indian Punjab, Sikh diaspora |
| Shahmukhi | 30.3 chars | 55.8 | 3.2 | Pakistani Punjab |
| Roman Punjabi | 36.0 chars | 36.0 | 2.7 | Anyone literate in English |

The takeaway inverts the usual assumption: Roman Punjabi is the *longest* of the three, running 16% more characters than the Gurmukhi original, and it is the only one guaranteed to render on an old phone.

## Punjabi is not a Sikh-only language, and that changes the wish

Most pages ranking for this query file Punjabi wishes under "Sikh birthday wishes". That conflation makes people send the wrong line.

Punjabi is spoken by Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims across two countries. On the census table Nazir and colleagues reproduce, Punjabi is the mother tongue of 44.15% of Pakistan's population against Urdu's 7.57% — the single largest speaker group in the language, and one whose birthday register does not include Sikh formulas.

The Gurmukhi script does have a Sikh origin; Kaur records that it was standardised in the 16th century to write the gurus' teachings, and *Gurmukhi* means "from the mouth of the Guru". A script's history is not the language's boundary.

Practically: use wish 5 (*Rabb*) as your default blessing and wish 6 (*Waheguru*) only for a Sikh family. Sending a Sikh salutation to a Punjabi Muslim colleague is the sort of small error that lands.

## The honorifics that decide whether the wish lands

Punjabi marks respect grammatically, so this is not decoration. Kaur is explicit that an elder is addressed in the plural: *tusi*, never *tu*, and *tuhanu* rather than *tainu* for "to you".

The suffix *ji* is the second lever, and it attaches to kinship terms as a matter of course — *mama ji*, *masi ji*. English has no equivalent, which is why an English wish run through a translator arrives flat.

Third, get the relation word right. Punjabi distinguishes a father's elder brother (*taiyah*) from his younger brother (*chacha*), and a mother's brother (*mama*) from a father's sister's husband (*phuphar*) — Kaur lists dozens. "Happy birthday uncle" collapses four people into one word; Punjabi does not let you.

For a friend rather than an elder, drop *ji* and use *tu* — over-formality reads as distance. A [birthday page for a friend](https://subhsandesh.in/birthday-friend) is the right place for that register, since the informal line and the inside joke can sit together.

## When a Punjabi birthday wish is the wrong choice

Sometimes it is. If the recipient speaks Punjabi but reads only Hindi or Urdu — common in urban families a generation out from Punjab — a Gurmukhi line is affection they cannot open. Send Roman, or a voice note.

Our own data argues for restraint. Of 195 SubhSandesh birthday pages that included a quiz, only 28 were ever played — 14.4%. Senders build more than recipients consume, and the same rule holds here: one correct line beats eight copied ones.

Birthday views on SubhSandesh are 48.6% mobile against 51.0% site-wide, so a Punjabi page is likelier than most to open on a laptop, where the installed Gurmukhi font is a coin toss. And 4 of 198 birthday pages were never opened at all.

If the relationship is thin, a script decision will not fix it — phone them and say *janamdin mubarak* out loud, because speech crosses the border writing cannot. If you do want the page, [browse the full template set](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) and paste the Gurmukhi line in.

- [Language Shift – The Case of Punjabi in Sargodha Region of Pakistan](https://journals.uni-lj.si/ala/article/view/183), *Acta Linguistica Asiatica* 3(2), 2013.
- [Word Disambiguation in Shahmukhi to Gurmukhi Transliteration](https://learnpunjabi.org/pdf/WSD%20in%20Gurmukhi-Shahmukhi%20Trans.pdf), Saini and Lehal, Punjabi University, Patiala. Proceedings of the 9th Workshop on Asian Language Resources, 12 November 2011.
- [Strategies and Approaches in Translating Cultural Punjabi Terms](https://ejournal.um.edu.my/index.php/JML/article/view/3716), Kulwindr Kaur, *Journal of Modern Languages* 18(1), 2008.

failed.why: The differentiating claim in this post IS the script content — the eight Gurmukhi wishes, their Roman transliterations, the tu/tusi and ji register guidance, and the character counts derived from those strings. Every Gurmukhi and Shahmukhi string here was machine-composed and is unverified: no agent can confirm Punjabi idiom, honorific register or Gurmukhi conjunct/diacritic correctness, so the claim is not yet established. Structural, not fixable by more work or another citation — a source can attest that Gurmukhi and Shahmukhi differ, but no source can attest that these particular sentences are idiomatic Punjabi. Closing condition: sign-off from a native Punjabi reader literate in Gurmukhi (and, for the Shahmukhi table row, in Shahmukhi) on each string before publish.
